current_episode.title: E422: Founding CIO of Berkeley Endowment on Track Records, Contrarian Investing & First-Time Funds

guest.bio_context: John Austin spent over 25 years as an investor, including serving as founding CIO at the Berkeley Endowment and previously as an investor at the Moore Foundation. He has extensive experience evaluating fund managers and developing investment criteria for institutional capital representing future generations.

context.transcript_excerpt: John Austin, you've spent over 25 years as an investor, including being founding CIO at the Berkeley Endowment. If you could point to one mistake that most GPs make over and over and over, what is that? The mistake that most GPs make is they have in their mind what they think is most important about their work, and they don't fully understand what an LP really cares about. And so they'll overemphasize things like track record or the fanciness of their bio. But what they really miss is what LPs really wanna hear, which is about them and their process. Why isn't track record the most important thing for a GP? Track records are part of the story for sure, but track records are inherently backward looking. And track records can be an artifact of what has happened, but as the old investment warning goes, past performance is not predictive necessarily of future results. That is 100% true. Track records will tell you who was there, what they did, how those things resulted, but that is an artifact of the time in which they were done. A good track record, to be really robust, you need to have a lot of transactions or a lot of data points. You need to have a consistent set of decision makers. You have to have a consistent set of market conditions. And that sort of thing isn't actually what you see in most track records. Most track records are folks over the course of different market conditions, over a course of different decision makers involved. And so a firm's track record is not as robust. What we wanna see from track record is evidence of an investment process at work that is compelling, that is repeatable, that is understandable. That's what we wanna see from a track record. If we see a track record that's a fantastic track record, but it's over too long a time period in an environment that's very different than today, it's a lot less reliable. So a good LP is going to look for what drove the track record. So in another way, if the track record was the exact environment, the same team previously that was starting to invest today, that track record would be highly predictive. I sometimes think about it as, you think of recording artists, like their best albums are usually their first couple albums. There's something about that alchemy of that time period where there's a certain group of people that come together at a certain moment that generate a certain set of results. They have a certain set of life experiences that they bring to that moment of running their firm and attacking the market in that moment. And so maybe you were terrific in the post-GFC period, and maybe that opportunity set made your investors tons and tons of money. Your work in that time period was terrific. That isn't necessarily the environment we're in today. And so if you were terrific in that period, are you necessarily terrific today? You could have firms have terrific track records from that time period who may be floundering today. Just to play devil's advocate, aren't there investors like Warren Buffett, like Ken Griffin, like Renaissance Technology that have these sustainable competitive advantages for many decades? Isn't that also pretty common? There are firms that have sustainable advantages. We feel like they're more common because they're famous. We all know who Warren Buffett is because there are 25 Warren Buffetts. There's one. And so there are firms that can create sustainable ed. pending_qa.q: How should limited partners evaluate the durability of a fund manager's investment process?
pending_qa.r: LPs should look at the number of investment decisions and transactions, not just the number of years. A hedge fund making hundreds of investments per day provides more data points than a private equity fund making a few investments per year. Durability comes from seeing the decision-making process repeat consistently across many investments.

pending_qa.q: What specific elements of a fund manager's investment process should a CIO examine?
pending_qa.r: A CIO should evaluate how managers source investments, how they evaluate opportunities, how they structure deals, what value-add they provide post-investment, and ultimately how they exit positions. Understanding these component pieces reveals where the firm creates value and what it is particularly good at.

pending_qa.q: How has the private markets landscape changed over the past 25 to 30 years for LPs?
pending_qa.r: The biggest change is the explosion of asset size and the number of firms competing for assets. Thirty years ago, a firm with liquidity had tremendous access to any fund they wanted; today it is much harder to find terrific firms because there are so many more firms chasing a more fixed pool of assets. Additionally, things that were great moneymakers 25-30 years ago are different today due to increased competitiveness.

pending_qa.q: What operational and strategic advantages do firms like Citadel have compared to traditional private equity or venture funds?
pending_qa.r: Citadel is fundamentally different because it makes hundreds of investments in an hour, whereas a private equity fund might make a few investments a year. This volume provides vastly more data points from which to evaluate decision-making consistency and durability of process.

pending_qa.q: What characteristics distinguish exceptional fund managers from merely adequate ones?
pending_qa.r: Exceptional managers know who they are, what their investment sweet spot is, and how they operate. They are learners who evolve, but they start from a sense of purpose and groundedness. They view themselves as stewards taking fiduciary responsibility seriously, which impacts how the firm behaves, respects LPs, and holds its team to standards.

pending_qa.q: Why is it critical for a fund manager to have a clear, documented investment process?
pending_qa.r: A clear process ensures the firm makes investments based on high conviction fit with their thesis, not deployment pressure. It also enables team clarity on strike zone and investment criteria so every team member understands what assets the firm targets and how they evaluate them. Without process, a firm is not really investing—it is just managing assets.

pending_qa.q: What is the relationship between investment rootedness and volatile asset performance?
pending_qa.r: Having rootedness in your investment thesis keeps you from making emotional decisions during volatility. Without rootedness, an investor who bought an asset at $10 and saw it rise 15x to $150 would sell when it drops 20% to lock in gains, missing the eventual much higher appreciation. Rootedness requires upfront work but prevents selling at the worst possible time.

pending_qa.q: What criteria should limited partners establish to identify fund managers worth backing?
pending_qa.r: LPs should look for alignment between the investment team and LP capital, clarity in how the manager communicates their strategy, and a true fiduciary mindset. An LP should develop a set of beliefs and characteristics that define what kind of firm to partner with—essentially a strike zone for LPs, just as fund managers should have their own investment strike zone.

pending_qa.q: How can LPs distinguish between a bad outcome and a bad investment decision when a fund underperforms?
pending_qa.r: LPs that have done deep work understanding the fund manager's process and sector context can separate temporary underperformance driven by environment from actual flawed decision-making. This knowledge allows them to stick with managers through rough patches and avoid panic selling based purely on poor results rather than evaluating the quality of the underlying decisions.
